items.readable_text:
Content:
For quadrantal angles that lie outside [MATH: [0^\circ,360^\circ),] we first find a coterminal angle in the interval [MATH: [0^\circ,360^\circ),] and then we proceed as usual.

Content:
For example, if the angle is [MATH: 540^\circ,] then we write
[MATH: 540^\circ - 360^\circ = 180^\circ.\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]
So [MATH: 180^\circ] is coterminal with [MATH: 540^\circ,] and we need to look at the point on the unit circle that corresponds to [MATH: 180^\circ,] which is [MATH: (-1,0).]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c020fed4f9fe4967fd23e61716442958]

Content:
We can do a similar thing when working with negative angles. For example, if the angle is [MATH: -\dfrac{7\pi}{2},] we can write
[MATH: − (7π)/(2) + 2π|= − (3π)/(2); − (3π)/(2) + 2π|= (π)/(2).✓]
So, we need to look at the point that corresponds to [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}2,] that is, [MATH: (0,1).]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we find an angle that's coterminal with [MATH: \dfrac{7\pi}{2}] and lies in the range [MATH: [0,2\pi).]

[MATH: (7π)/(2) − 2π|= (3π)/(2)✓]

Therefore, [MATH: \sin \left(\dfrac{7\pi}2\right) = \sin \left(\dfrac{3\pi}2\right).]

The angle [MATH: \dfrac{3\pi}{2}] is a quadrantal angle. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

From the unit circle, we see that the angle [MATH: \dfrac{3\pi}{2}] corresponds to the point [MATH: (0,-1).]

Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the [MATH: y]-coordinate, we have [MATH: \sin{\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right)} = -1.]

Therefore, [MATH: \sin \left(\dfrac{7\pi}2\right) = -1.]

items.title: Computing the Trigonometric Ratio of a Negative Quadrantal Angle

sections.normalized_html:
First, we find an angle that's coterminal with [MATH: -270^\circ] that lies in the range [MATH: [0^\circ, 360^\circ).]

[MATH: -270^\circ + 360^\circ = 90^\circ\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]

Therefore, [MATH: \cot\left(-270^\circ\right) = \cot{90^\circ}.]

The angle [MATH: 90^\circ] is a quadrantal angle. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

From the unit circle, we see that the angle [MATH: 90^\circ] corresponds to the point [MATH: (0,1).]

  • Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the [MATH: x]-coordinate, we have [MATH: \cos{90^\circ} = 0.]

  • Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the [MATH: y]-coordinate, we have [MATH: \sin{90^\circ} = 1.]

So, using the fact that [MATH: \cot{\theta} = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta},] we have

[MATH: \cot{90^\circ} = \dfrac{\cos{90^\circ}}{\sin{90^\circ}} = \dfrac{0}{1}.]

Therefore, [MATH: \cot(-270^\circ) =0.]
